options.a: Annual reviews with forced distribution curves applied across teams
options.b: Rating scales expanded from five points to ten for finer distinctions
options.c: Continuous feedback, goal agility, and development focus
options.d: Self-appraisals replacing manager reviews and goal-setting meetings

distractorExplanations.a: Forced-distribution annual reviews are the legacy model that modernization moves away from, not the destination.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding rating points refines the annual rating event; modernization shifts emphasis to ongoing feedback and development.
distractorExplanations.d: Dropping manager input and goal meetings removes coaching; modern systems increase manager-employee conversations.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-people-001.explanation: Modern performance systems emphasize ongoing coaching and aligned goals. The shift is away from annual, rank-only reviews.

options.a: Internal pay history, incumbent tenure, and last year's merit increase budget
options.b: National unemployment rate and general CPI inflation figures only
options.c: Career-site posting views, employee referral counts, and offer acceptance rates
options.d: Competitor pay, pipeline data, geographic differentials, and time-to-fill trends

distractorExplanations.a: Internal pay history and merit budgets are inward-looking; scarce-skill analysis needs external competitor and supply data.
distractorExplanations.b: Headline unemployment and CPI are too broad; scarce skills require role-specific pay, pipeline, and geographic data.
distractorExplanations.c: Career-site and referral metrics describe your own funnel, not the external labor market for the scarce skill.

options.a: Surveys, focus groups, stay/exit interviews, and action planning
options.b: An annual engagement census with results reported to senior leaders
options.c: Anonymous suggestion boxes and an open-door policy for concerns
options.d: Pulse surveys, sentiment dashboards, and external benchmark scores

distractorExplanations.b: A census reported upward collects data but closes no loop; listening strategy requires action planning back to employees.
distractorExplanations.c: Passive channels wait for employees to speak up; a listening strategy actively gathers input and acts on it.
distractorExplanations.d: More collection tools and benchmarks still lack action planning, the step that makes listening credible to employees.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-people-003.explanation: Listening systems require closure loops demonstrating leadership response. Action planning needs owners and accountability so employees see results.

options.a: Remove degree requirements from postings while keeping old screening
options.b: Redesign job architecture, assessments, and manager enablement
options.c: Add a skills keyword filter to the applicant tracking screen
options.d: Require industry certifications in place of degrees for every role

distractorExplanations.a: Dropping degrees from postings while screens still favor degrees is cosmetic; assessments and job architecture must change.
distractorExplanations.c: Keyword filters automate resume matching, not validated skills assessment, and leave job architecture unchanged.
distractorExplanations.d: Swapping degrees for certifications replaces one credential filter with another instead of assessing demonstrated skills.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-people-004.explanation: Skills-based approaches need job profiles, validated assessments, and bias mitigation. The goal is moving away from degree-only filters.

options.a: Higher external applicant volume and stronger employer brand reach
options.b: Replacement of formal succession planning for executive roles
options.c: Retention, skill deployment, and reduced time-to-productivity
options.d: Standardized pay grades and fewer job titles across the company

distractorExplanations.a: Marketplaces match internal talent to work; external applicant volume is a recruitment marketing outcome.
distractorExplanations.b: Gig and project matching complements, not replaces, succession planning for executive and critical roles.
distractorExplanations.d: Fewer titles and standard grades come from job architecture work, not from an internal talent marketplace.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-people-005.explanation: Marketplaces match employees to gigs/projects developing careers and agility. These gains show up on project and gig assignments.

options.a: Business strategy, future skill needs, and demographic trends
options.b: Current headcount budget, open requisitions, and this year's attrition
options.c: Last year's org chart, historical staffing ratios, and current titles
options.d: Competitor headcount levels, industry ratios, and peer spans of control

distractorExplanations.b: Budget, open reqs, and current attrition are operational staffing inputs; strategic planning looks multi-year at business strategy and future skills.
distractorExplanations.c: Replicating historical structure and ratios is backward-looking; strategic plans start from where the business is going, not where it was.
distractorExplanations.d: Benchmarks are context, not the anchor; strategic workforce plans align to this organization's own strategy and future skill needs.

options.a: Survey participation rate compared with last year's response rate
options.b: Trends in engagement survey scores linked to turnover and productivity
options.c: Number of engagement events held and attendance at each session
options.d: Single-year average engagement score compared against external industry norms

distractorExplanations.a: Response rate measures survey reach, not whether engagement is improving or driving retention and productivity outcomes.
distractorExplanations.c: Event counts and attendance are activity measures; effectiveness requires engagement trends tied to turnover and productivity.
distractorExplanations.d: A one-year snapshot benchmarked externally shows no trend and no link to business outcomes such as turnover or output.

options.a: Naming one replacement per role based on the incumbent's preference
options.b: Filling critical roles through external searches once vacancies post
options.c: Identifying high-potential talent and development plans
options.d: Ranking current employees by tenure to set the order of promotions

distractorExplanations.a: That is narrow replacement planning driven by one person's opinion, not assessed high-potential pools with development plans.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for a vacancy and then searching externally is reactive staffing, the opposite of building ready-now internal successors.
distractorExplanations.d: Seniority ordering ignores potential and readiness; succession planning assesses capability and closes gaps through development.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-people-008.explanation: Effective succession identifies roles, competencies, and development pipelines proactively. Development plans close gaps so successors reach readiness.

options.a: Base salary, short-term incentives, and long-term incentives
options.b: Benefits, perks, and wellness programs managed apart from pay
options.c: Base pay ranges, merit budgets, and market pricing of jobs
options.d: Compensation, benefits, recognition, and career opportunities

distractorExplanations.a: Base plus short- and long-term incentives is total direct compensation, only one element of a total rewards framework.
distractorExplanations.b: Managing benefits separately from pay is the siloed approach total rewards replaces; it also omits recognition and careers.
distractorExplanations.c: Ranges, merit budgets, and pricing describe compensation structure, not the integrated pay-benefits-recognition-career offer.

options.a: Embed in talent processes, leadership accountability, and measurable outcomes
options.b: Center on annual awareness training and heritage-month events led by HR
options.c: Treat EEO-1 reporting and affirmative action plan filings as the end goal
options.d: Be delegated to employee resource groups that own the goals and budget

distractorExplanations.b: Awareness events are activities without accountability or measured outcomes; strategic DEI is embedded in talent processes.
distractorExplanations.c: EEO-1 and AAP filings are compliance floors; strategic DEI goes beyond legal minimums to leadership accountability and results.
distractorExplanations.d: ERGs support inclusion but cannot own enterprise accountability; leaders and talent processes must carry DEI outcomes.

options.a: Assessing potential separately from current performance ratings
options.b: Bias by using clear criteria, diverse slate review, and transparent process
options.c: Linking selection criteria to business-critical future leadership competencies
options.d: Using stretch assignments and job rotations as development experiences

distractorExplanations.a: Separating potential from performance (e.g., nine-box) is recommended practice, so it is something to keep, not avoid.
distractorExplanations.c: Tying HiPo criteria to business-critical competencies is good design that reduces bias; it should be kept, not avoided.
distractorExplanations.d: Stretch assignments and rotations are core HiPo development methods; avoiding them would weaken the program.

options.a: Overall annual turnover rate compared with the industry average
options.b: Time-to-fill and cost-per-hire for roles vacated during last year
options.c: Headcount growth by department and the HR-to-employee staffing ratio
options.d: Regrettable turnover by role, tenure, manager, and exit interview themes

distractorExplanations.a: An aggregate turnover rate hides who is leaving and why; retention analytics segments regrettable loss by role and manager.
distractorExplanations.b: Time-to-fill and cost-per-hire are recruiting efficiency metrics; they measure backfill, not the drivers of departures.
distractorExplanations.c: Headcount growth and HR staffing ratios are workforce size and HR efficiency measures, not retention driver analysis.

options.a: Behavior change, leadership 360 improvements, and business unit outcomes
options.b: Coachee satisfaction ratings collected right after the final coaching session
options.c: Number of sessions completed and hours logged on the contract
options.d: Coach credentials, certification hours, and assessment tools used

distractorExplanations.b: Satisfaction is Kirkpatrick Level 1 (reaction); ROI needs behavior change and business results, not how the coachee felt.
distractorExplanations.c: Sessions and hours are activity inputs; they show the coaching happened, not that leadership behavior or results changed.
distractorExplanations.d: Coach qualifications are inputs that predict quality; they do not demonstrate any return from the engagement.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-people-014.explanation: Coaching impact measured through leadership behaviors and downstream results. Outcomes should be tracked over time, not just at the end of the engagement.

options.a: Relocation lump sum, home payroll exit, and a one-way permanent move package
options.b: Tax, immigration, compensation COLA, family support, and repatriation
options.c: Host-country salary only, with home pension and benefits ended
options.d: Business-travel per diems and visa rules for trips under 90 days

distractorExplanations.a: A one-way lump-sum move is a permanent transfer/localization package; long-term assignments also need repatriation planning.
distractorExplanations.c: Switching to host pay and ending home benefits is localization, not a long-term assignment policy with COLA and return.
distractorExplanations.d: Per diems and short-trip visa rules govern business travel, not multi-year assignments with tax, family, and repatriation needs.

options.a: Stakeholder impact, capacity for change, and risks to adoption
options.b: Project budget, milestone dates, and vendor delivery schedules
options.c: Post-launch adoption rates and help-desk ticket volumes
options.d: Employee satisfaction with pay, benefits, and working conditions

distractorExplanations.b: Budget and milestones are project management controls; readiness assesses people impact and capacity to adopt.
distractorExplanations.c: Adoption and ticket data are measured after go-live; readiness assessment happens before launch to plan support.
distractorExplanations.d: Satisfaction with pay and conditions is an engagement survey topic, not stakeholder impact or change capacity.

options.a: Annual voluntary turnover, cost of turnover, and exit counts
options.b: Quality of hire, internal fill rate, and time-to-productivity
options.c: Total HR cost per employee and the HR-to-employee staff ratio
options.d: Prior-year absenteeism rate and workers' comp claim totals

distractorExplanations.a: Turnover rate, cost, and exits are lagging indicators; they report losses that have already happened.
distractorExplanations.c: HR cost and staffing ratios are efficiency measures reported after the fact, not predictors of workforce performance.
distractorExplanations.d: Prior-year absence and claims totals are lagging outcomes; leading indicators predict future capability.

options.a: Detailed multi-year project plans approved before any design begins
options.b: Specialist HR teams handing work off in sequence from one function to the next
options.c: Iterative releases, cross-functional squads, and customer feedback loops
options.d: Annual policy reviews with changes released after full sign-off

distractorExplanations.a: Big up-front multi-year plans are waterfall; agile HR releases small increments and adjusts from feedback.
distractorExplanations.b: Sequential handoffs between specialist silos are what cross-functional agile squads are designed to remove.
distractorExplanations.d: Annual release cycles after full sign-off are the opposite of iterative releases tested with employees.

options.a: One global pay range per level converted at current exchange rates
options.b: Separate leveling systems built by each country HR team
options.c: Job titles matched to the nearest local survey title only
options.d: Consistent job leveling framework with local market pricing

distractorExplanations.a: A single converted range ignores local labor markets; leveling should be global while pricing stays local.
distractorExplanations.b: Country-specific leveling breaks comparability across borders, undermining global internal equity.
distractorExplanations.c: Title matching without a common leveling framework lets title inflation drive grades instead of job content.

options.a: Executive sponsorship, SLAs, change management, and technology enablement
options.b: Lift-and-shift of current HR tasks to a low-cost site before redesign
options.c: Headcount reduction targets used as the primary measure of success
options.d: A new HR portal launched first, with service standards set later

distractorExplanations.b: Moving work without redesigning processes relocates inefficiency; SSCs need standardization and change management.
distractorExplanations.c: Cost cuts alone ignore SLAs and customer experience, so service quality and adoption suffer.
distractorExplanations.d: Launching technology before SLAs and governance leaves no service standard for the portal to deliver.

options.a: Apply across-the-board percentage cuts to each department equally
options.b: Model multiple options with impact on capability, DEI, and employer brand
options.c: Base reductions on last-in, first-out seniority order to limit legal exposure
options.d: Choose the option with the largest short-term payroll savings

distractorExplanations.a: Uniform cuts ignore which capabilities are critical; scenario planning compares options by impact before acting.
distractorExplanations.c: LIFO can still create disparate impact (e.g., on recent diverse hires) and ignores capability; it is not risk-free.
distractorExplanations.d: Maximizing immediate savings ignores capability loss, DEI impact, and employer brand that scenario models weigh.

options.a: Headcount growth rate, spans of control, and office capacity
options.b: Revenue per employee and gross margin shifts by business unit
options.c: Values drift, decision bottlenecks, and inclusion gaps
options.d: Compliance training completion and policy acknowledgment rates

distractorExplanations.a: Headcount and spans are structural metrics; culture diagnostics look at values, decision norms, and inclusion.
distractorExplanations.b: Revenue and margin are financial productivity results, not evidence of values drift or inclusion gaps.
distractorExplanations.d: Completion and acknowledgment rates show compliance activity, not how culture has shifted during growth.

options.a: Selecting the top-rated vendor in each category from analyst reports
options.b: Letting each region choose its own HRIS to match local practice
options.c: Feature checklists compared on price before process mapping
options.d: Integration architecture, data governance, and user adoption planning

distractorExplanations.a: Best-of-breed picks from analyst rankings create disconnected point solutions without an integration architecture.
distractorExplanations.b: Regional HRIS choices duplicate systems and fragment data governance, defeating an aligned roadmap.
distractorExplanations.c: Buying on features and price before mapping processes skips integration, data governance, and adoption planning.

options.a: Consulting on workforce implications of business decisions
options.b: Processing employee transactions and answering policy questions
options.c: Designing enterprise compensation programs as the pay specialist
options.d: Policing policy compliance and handling discipline paperwork

distractorExplanations.b: Transactions and policy queries belong to shared services in the three-pillar model, not the HRBP role.
distractorExplanations.c: Program design is the center of excellence role; HRBPs consult on business decisions using CoE expertise.
distractorExplanations.d: Policing rules is a compliance/employee-relations function; strategic HRBPs advise leaders on workforce implications.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-organization-009.explanation: Strategic HRBPs co-create workforce plans tied to business outcomes. HRBPs ground that advice in workforce data.

options.a: Exit interviews held during the expert's final week on the job
options.b: Documentation, mentoring, and phased transition plans
options.c: Hiring an external replacement after the expert has retired
options.d: A shared drive where the expert uploads files before leaving

distractorExplanations.a: A final-week exit interview is too late and too short to transfer tacit expertise built over years.
distractorExplanations.c: Backfilling after departure loses the expert's tacit knowledge; transfer must happen before the exit.
distractorExplanations.d: Uploading files captures explicit documents only; mentoring and phased handover transfer tacit know-how.

options.a: Formal reporting lines and approved spans of control
options.b: Individual performance ratings and potential scores
options.c: Informal influencers and collaboration bottlenecks
options.d: Engagement survey scores broken out by team and site

distractorExplanations.a: Formal lines and spans come from the org chart; ONA exists to reveal the informal networks the chart misses.
distractorExplanations.b: Ratings and potential come from talent reviews, not from mapping who collaborates and communicates with whom.
distractorExplanations.d: Engagement scores measure attitudes by unit; ONA maps relationships, influencers, and bottlenecks.

options.a: A single CEO email, with details shared only after final decisions
options.b: Team-specific messages that each manager drafts in their own words
options.c: Waiting to announce until every individual role decision is made
options.d: Timely, empathetic, consistent messages with manager talking points

distractorExplanations.a: One email with details withheld leaves a vacuum filled by rumor; managers need timely, consistent talking points.
distractorExplanations.b: Letting each manager improvise produces inconsistent stories; core messages should be shared with talking points.
distractorExplanations.c: Delaying until every decision is final fuels rumors; timely communication shares what is known and when more will come.

options.a: Set standards, provide expert consulting, and govern pay programs
options.b: Process payroll changes and answer employee pay questions directly
options.c: Approve each individual offer in place of HRBPs and hiring managers
options.d: Let business units set pay without central guidelines or review

distractorExplanations.b: Payroll processing and employee queries are shared services work, not the CoE's expert design and governance role.
distractorExplanations.c: Approving every offer centralizes transactions in the CoE; it should set guidelines and govern, not replace managers.
distractorExplanations.d: Removing central guidelines abandons the CoE's governance role and invites inconsistent, inequitable pay.

options.a: Fully autonomous country HR teams, each with its own policies
options.b: Centers of excellence, HRBPs, and shared services with defined RACI
options.c: A single corporate HR team serving every country directly from headquarters
options.d: An outsourced global PEO handling HR delivery in each country

distractorExplanations.a: Fully decentralized country HR duplicates work and loses global standards that the three-pillar model provides.
distractorExplanations.c: Pure centralization lacks local business partnering and country compliance expertise.
distractorExplanations.d: A PEO can support employment in some countries but does not replace CoEs, HRBPs, and shared services governance.

options.a: Adopting the acquirer's structure and policies in every unit on day one
options.b: Cost synergies through headcount cuts before critical roles are mapped
options.c: Running both legacy structures in parallel until the next fiscal year
options.d: Clarity of reporting, decision rights, and critical role retention

distractorExplanations.a: Imposing the acquirer's full structure on day one ignores critical-role retention and creates avoidable talent loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Cutting before mapping critical roles and decision rights risks losing the talent the deal was meant to capture.
distractorExplanations.c: Parallel structures leave reporting lines and decision rights unclear, the opposite of integration clarity.

options.a: Examining acceptable documents within required timeframe without discrimination
options.b: Requesting a U.S. passport or green card from each non-citizen new hire
options.c: Completing Section 2 at the offer stage to screen out unauthorized applicants
options.d: Reverifying every employee's identity documents each year on the anniversary

distractorExplanations.b: Demanding specific documents is document abuse under INA 274B; the employee chooses from the Lists of Acceptable Documents.
distractorExplanations.c: Section 2 is completed within 3 business days after the start date; using I-9 to prescreen applicants is prohibited.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverification applies only when temporary work authorization expires, never to identity documents on a yearly cycle.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-workplace-001.explanation: I-9 process verifies identity and work authorization uniformly. National origin and citizenship discrimination in the I-9 process is unlawful.

options.a: Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, and age
options.b: Race, color, religion, disability, and national origin
options.c: Race, color, religion, sex, and national origin
options.d: Race, color, sex, genetic information, and veteran status

distractorExplanations.a: Age is protected by the ADEA (40 and over), not Title VII, which lists race, color, religion, sex, and national origin.
distractorExplanations.b: Disability is protected by the ADA, not Title VII; Title VII's fifth class is sex, not disability.
distractorExplanations.d: Genetic information is a GINA protection and veteran status falls under USERRA/VEVRAA; Title VII also covers religion.

options.a: Granting the exact accommodation the employee requests if reasonable
options.b: A doctor's note confirming disability before any discussion begins
options.c: Accommodation only after the employee completes the probationary period
options.d: Interactive dialogue to identify effective accommodation unless undue hardship

distractorExplanations.a: The employer may choose among effective accommodations; it need not grant the employee's preferred option.
distractorExplanations.b: Documentation may be requested when disability is not obvious, but it is part of the interactive process, not a gate to it.
distractorExplanations.c: ADA duties apply to applicants and new hires from day one; probation does not delay the obligation.

options.a: 50+ employees within 75 miles, 12 months service, 1250 hours worked
options.b: 15+ employees within 50 miles, 6 months service, 1000 hours worked
options.c: 20+ employees within 75 miles, 12 months service, 1000 hours worked
options.d: 50+ employees within 100 miles, 12 months service, 1500 hours worked

distractorExplanations.b: 15 employees is the Title VII/ADA coverage threshold; FMLA needs 50 within 75 miles, 12 months, and 1,250 hours.
distractorExplanations.c: 20 employees is the ADEA threshold and 1,000 hours is an ERISA plan-participation figure; FMLA requires 50 and 1,250.
distractorExplanations.d: Radius and hours are wrong: FMLA counts 50 employees within 75 miles and requires 1,250 hours in the prior 12 months.

options.a: Annual training sign-offs relied on as the employer's main legal defense
options.b: Policy, training, investigation protocol, and leadership accountability
options.c: Investigating only complaints that are submitted in writing
options.d: Reporting routed through the direct supervisor as the single channel

distractorExplanations.a: Training alone does not establish the Faragher/Ellerth defense; policy, complaint handling, and corrective action are needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Employers must act on harassment they know or should know about, including verbal reports, not just written complaints.
distractorExplanations.d: A supervisor-only channel fails when the supervisor is the harasser; policies need multiple reporting avenues.

options.a: Company-wide average pay by gender without job or level controls
options.b: Base salary gaps only, with bonuses and equity excluded from scope
options.c: Comp gaps controlling for role, level, experience, and performance
options.d: Starting-salary gaps compared against prior-employer pay history

distractorExplanations.a: Raw averages mix different jobs and levels; equity analysis controls for legitimate factors to find unexplained gaps.
distractorExplanations.b: Excluding incentives misses common sources of disparity; total cash and equity should be in scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Prior pay can carry past discrimination forward and many states ban salary-history use; it is not a valid control.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-workplace-006.explanation: Regression or cohort analysis identifies unexplained pay disparities. Performance is a valid control only where ratings themselves are unbiased.

options.a: Address hazards only when a specific OSHA standard covers them
options.b: Report every recordable injury to OSHA within eight hours
options.c: Eliminate every minor hazard, even where abatement is infeasible
options.d: Provide workplace free from recognized serious hazards

distractorExplanations.a: The general duty clause exists precisely to cover recognized serious hazards that no specific standard addresses.
distractorExplanations.b: Eight-hour reporting applies to fatalities (24 hours for in-patient hospitalization, amputation, eye loss), not all recordables.
distractorExplanations.c: The clause targets recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious harm with feasible abatement, not every minor risk.

options.a: Threaten, surveil, or discriminate for protected concerted activity
options.b: Share factual information about unions and dues with employees
options.c: Express its opinion against unionization without threats or promises
options.d: Enforce neutral no-solicitation rules limited to working time

distractorExplanations.b: Factual statements about unions and dues are protected employer speech under Section 8(c) when free of threats or promises.
distractorExplanations.c: Section 8(c) lets employers voice anti-union views as long as there is no threat, interrogation, promise, or surveillance.
distractorExplanations.d: Neutral working-time solicitation rules, applied consistently, are lawful; unlawful rules target union activity or break time.

options.a: Headquarters-state wage, tax, and leave rules for each remote worker
options.b: Tax, wage/hour, workers' comp, and benefits jurisdiction issues
options.c: Federal FLSA rules alone, since state law yields to federal standards
options.d: Only income tax withholding, as wage/hour rules follow the employer

distractorExplanations.a: Employment law generally follows where the employee works, so HQ-state rules do not govern remote staff in other states.
distractorExplanations.c: The FLSA is a floor; more protective state wage-hour laws (minimum wage, overtime, pay timing) still apply.
distractorExplanations.d: Wage/hour, workers' comp, and leave laws follow the work location, so tax withholding is only one jurisdictional issue.

options.a: Zero-tolerance termination for any threat, without assessment
options.b: Badge access and security camera upgrades as the core of the program
options.c: Risk assessment, reporting, training, and coordination with security
options.d: Responding after incidents occur through police reports and claims

distractorExplanations.a: Automatic termination skips threat assessment and can escalate risk; programs assess, intervene, and coordinate.
distractorExplanations.b: Physical security is one control; prevention also needs risk assessment, reporting channels, and training.
distractorExplanations.d: A purely reactive approach misses prevention steps such as hazard assessment, threat reporting, and training.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-workplace-010.explanation: WVPP identifies hazards, trains response, and protects reporters. Coordination with law enforcement is part of the response plan.

options.a: Be led by the accused's manager, who knows the team dynamics best
options.b: Promise complete confidentiality to the complainant and witnesses
options.c: Wait until an EEOC charge is filed before interviewing witnesses
options.d: Be prompt, impartial, documented, and lead to appropriate action

distractorExplanations.a: The accused's manager has a conflict of interest; investigators must be impartial and trained.
distractorExplanations.b: Investigators cannot promise total confidentiality; information is shared on a need-to-know basis to act.
distractorExplanations.c: The duty to investigate starts with the internal complaint; waiting for a charge undermines the employer's defense.

options.a: Protection applies only if the reported violation is later proven
options.b: Internal complaints to a supervisor fall outside legal protection
options.c: Retaliation prohibited; reports should go through defined channels
options.d: Retaliation complaints under the OSH Act are filed within 180 days

distractorExplanations.a: Protection covers good-faith reports; the hazard need not be proven for retaliation to be unlawful.
distractorExplanations.b: OSH Act Section 11(c) protects internal safety complaints to management as well as complaints to OSHA.
distractorExplanations.d: OSH Act 11(c) retaliation complaints must be filed within 30 days; 180 days applies to statutes such as SOX.

options.a: A substitute for the ADA interactive accommodation process
options.b: A required referral step before any disciplinary action
options.c: Manager access to session notes to support performance plans
options.d: Early intervention for mental health/substance issues

distractorExplanations.a: An EAP referral does not satisfy ADA duties; accommodation still requires the interactive process.
distractorExplanations.b: EAP referral can be offered alongside discipline but is not a legal prerequisite for performance management.
distractorExplanations.c: EAP sessions are confidential; managers do not get session content, which would destroy employee trust and use.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-workplace-015.explanation: EAP supports wellbeing confidentially; not substitute for accommodation or performance management. Early intervention reduces absenteeism and turnover.

options.a: Team members are shielded from accountability for missed goals
options.b: Team members can raise concerns without fear of retaliation
options.c: Leaders avoid critical feedback to keep the team comfortable
options.d: Decisions require consensus so no one ever feels overruled

distractorExplanations.a: Psychological safety pairs candor with high standards; it does not remove accountability for performance.
distractorExplanations.c: Avoiding hard feedback is comfort, not safety; safe teams can discuss problems and mistakes openly.
distractorExplanations.d: Safety means voicing dissent without fear; it does not require consensus decision-making.

options.a: Benefit plan costs, pension liabilities, and severance obligations
options.b: Pending employment litigation and wage-hour audit exposure in the target
options.c: Leadership styles, decision norms, and integration risk
options.d: Headcount, payroll totals, and union contracts at the target firm

distractorExplanations.a: Benefit and pension liabilities belong to financial HR due diligence, not cultural due diligence.
distractorExplanations.b: Litigation and wage-hour exposure are legal due diligence items, not leadership style or decision norms.
distractorExplanations.d: Headcount, payroll, and labor agreements are HR data-room items; culture review looks at norms and leadership.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-strategy-002.explanation: Culture clash drives deal failure; HR assesses alignment and integration plan. The key integration risk is losing critical talent.

options.a: Constant availability to executives to show commitment
options.b: Handling high-stakes cases alone to protect confidentiality
options.c: Taking leave only after major crises are fully resolved
options.d: Boundaries, peer support, and continuous learning

distractorExplanations.a: Unlimited availability without recovery leads to burnout and impaired judgment, the opposite of resilience.
distractorExplanations.b: Confidentiality does not require isolation; peer support and counsel are core resilience resources.
distractorExplanations.c: Deferring recovery until crises end means it rarely happens; boundaries need to be sustained continuously.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-strategy-003.explanation: Sustainable leadership practices prevent burnout and support sound judgment. These practices sustain effectiveness over time.

options.a: Present HR program activity counts and participation statistics
options.b: Benchmark HR spend against peers and request a matching budget
options.c: Translate people metrics into business risk and ROI narratives
options.d: Lead with best-practice research and employee sentiment quotes

distractorExplanations.a: Activity counts show HR effort, not business impact; executives fund initiatives tied to risk and ROI.
distractorExplanations.b: Peer spend parity is not a business case; investment should be justified by risk reduction and returns.
distractorExplanations.d: Research and quotes support a case but do not translate people data into the financial and risk terms executives use.

options.a: Individual performance ratings for each employee below executives
options.b: Detailed HR department budget variances and HR team headcount by function
options.c: Employee benefit claims data broken out by named plan participants
options.d: Turnover, leadership bench strength, culture indicators, and DEI progress

distractorExplanations.a: Boards oversee strategic human capital risk, not individual ratings, which belong to management.
distractorExplanations.b: HR's own operating budget is a management detail; boards need enterprise talent risk and culture indicators.
distractorExplanations.c: Identified health claims data raises HIPAA/privacy issues and is not strategic oversight information.

options.a: Compassionate communication, compliance, outplacement support, and survivor care
options.b: Fast, uniform email notices to impacted staff to limit disruption on site
options.c: WARN notice given 30 days ahead for qualifying plant closings and layoffs
options.d: Severance in exchange for releases, with survivors briefed weeks later

distractorExplanations.b: Email-only notice without trained managers damages trust; people should hear the news in a humane conversation.
distractorExplanations.c: Federal WARN requires 60 days' notice for covered closings and mass layoffs, not 30 days.
distractorExplanations.d: Neglecting survivors erodes engagement and retention; survivor communication should happen right away.

options.a: Office lease renewals, IT hardware refresh cycles, and rising facilities costs
options.b: Critical skill gaps, compliance failures, and culture/ reputational threats
options.c: Completed HR projects, closed audit findings, and resolved grievances
options.d: Market share shifts, pricing pressure, and product launch delay risks

distractorExplanations.a: Leases, hardware, and facilities are operational/finance risks, not workforce-related strategic HR risks.
distractorExplanations.c: Closed items are history; a risk register lists open, forward-looking threats with likelihood and impact.
distractorExplanations.d: Market and product risks belong to commercial risk owners, not the workforce section of the register.

options.a: Private feedback only, given the executive's revenue contribution
options.b: A lateral move to a role with fewer direct reports to limit exposure
options.c: Clear expectations, consequences, and alignment with board
options.d: A 360 review shared with the executive, without any follow-up plan

distractorExplanations.a: Exempting high performers from consequences signals tolerance of misconduct and raises legal and culture risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving the executive relocates the behavior without expectations or consequences, passing harm to a new team.
distractorExplanations.d: Feedback without clear expectations, consequences, and follow-up rarely changes entrenched behavior.

shrm-cp-readiness-check-strategy-009.explanation: Senior leaders accountable; documented performance improvement or separation may be needed. Board alignment matters most if the behavior persists after coaching.

options.a: Deploy the headquarters curriculum unchanged to keep standards consistent
options.b: Train high-potentials at headquarters, then rely on expatriate leaders
options.c: Translate HQ materials into local languages as the main adaptation
options.d: Include cross-cultural competence, local mentorship, and inclusive cohort design

distractorExplanations.a: Unadapted HQ content ignores local context and cultural norms, reducing relevance and transfer.
distractorExplanations.b: Relying on expatriates blocks local leaders from the pipeline that emerging-market programs should build.
distractorExplanations.c: Translation alone changes language, not content, examples, mentorship, or cross-cultural competence.

options.a: Supplying verified human capital metrics for social disclosures
options.b: Owning carbon emissions data for the environmental disclosures
options.c: Drafting board independence and audit committee disclosures
options.d: Publishing engagement survey results as the full social disclosure

distractorExplanations.b: Emissions data sits in the environmental pillar with sustainability/operations, not HR's social metrics.
distractorExplanations.c: Board independence and audit committee items are governance disclosures led by legal/corporate secretary.
distractorExplanations.d: Engagement scores are one input; social disclosures cover workforce composition, safety, pay, and training.

options.a: A single forecast with full rollout as soon as the budget is approved
options.b: Scenario analysis, pilot programs, and staged investment with KPIs
options.c: Adopting the practices of the top competitor in the industry
options.d: Deferring decisions until market conditions become predictable

distractorExplanations.a: One forecast and a full rollout bet everything on one outcome; uncertainty calls for scenarios and staged pilots.
distractorExplanations.c: Copying a competitor ignores your own context and tests nothing before committing resources.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for certainty forfeits time; staged, measured investments let HR act while learning.

options.a: An HR-led program with leaders informed once the design is final
options.b: A CEO announcement and new values posters displayed at each site
options.c: Executive sponsors, manager enablement, and employee champions
options.d: Consultants who design and run the change program for leadership

distractorExplanations.a: Culture change led by HR alone lacks executive sponsorship; leaders must co-own it from the start.
distractorExplanations.b: Announcements and posters communicate but do not build the manager and employee coalition that sustains change.
distractorExplanations.d: Outsourcing ownership to consultants leaves no internal sponsors or champions once the engagement ends.

options.a: Back the CEO's growth plan, since the CEO sets company strategy
options.b: Apply the CFO's cut target evenly and protect HR's own budget
options.c: Defer both requests until the next annual budget planning cycle begins
options.d: Present workforce scenarios showing tradeoffs in capability and risk

distractorExplanations.a: Siding with one executive abandons HR's role of informing the decision with workforce data on both options.
distractorExplanations.b: Even cuts ignore capability tradeoffs, and protecting HR's budget is self-interest, not strategic advice.
distractorExplanations.c: Delay leaves the conflict unresolved; HR should frame scenarios now so leaders can decide on tradeoffs.

options.a: Business acumen, ethics, global/compliance expertise, and culture leadership
options.b: Deep HR technical expertise and many years spent in HR operations roles
options.c: The outgoing CHRO's chosen successor from among direct reports
options.d: Experience as the top HRBP to the CEO, with board-facing exposure not required

distractorExplanations.b: Functional depth alone is insufficient; the CHRO must be an enterprise leader with business acumen.
distractorExplanations.c: Deferring to the incumbent's pick is not board evaluation against enterprise competencies and ethics.
distractorExplanations.d: Board-facing experience matters for a CHRO, who advises on executive pay, succession, and governance.
